contents.name: Chapter 0 contents: "Cell Complexes", "Operations on Spaces", "Two Criteria for Homotopy Equivalence", and "The Homotopy Extension Property"
Cell Complexes: characteristic-map attachment and the definition of a CW complex
Cell Complexes: open cells, characteristic maps, and the warning that a closed cell need not be a closed ball
Cell Complexes: closure-finiteness and weak-topology conditions
Cell Complexes: skeleta and subcomplexes
Cell Complexes: the example showing a cell closure need not be a subcomplex
Operations on Spaces: products of cell complexes
Operations on Spaces: wedges, quotients by subcomplexes, and cell attachments
Two Criteria for Homotopy Equivalence
contents.reason: The Whitehead-style homotopy-equivalence criteria require a homotopy-group and cellular-approximation development that this homology construction neither assumes nor uses.

contents.name: The Homotopy Extension Property: Proposition 0.16 and the homotopy extension property for relative cell complexes
The Homotopy Extension Property: Proposition 0.19 and Corollaries 0.20--0.21
contents.reason: These relative-equivalence and mapping-cylinder consequences are not needed to form the skeletal filtration or identify its singular homology, so they would be an unused homotopy branch.

contents.name: Section 2.2 heading "Cellular Homology"
Cellular Homology: relative groups H_n(X^n,X^(n-1)) are free on n-cells and vanish away from n
Cellular Homology: construction of the cellular boundary from three consecutive skeleta and d squared equals zero
Theorem 2.35: cellular homology is isomorphic to singular homology
Immediate applications after Theorem 2.35: no n-cells, at most k generators, and no cells in adjacent dimensions
Cellular Homology: degree formula for cellular boundary coefficients
Example 2.36: closed orientable surfaces
Example 2.37: closed nonorientable surfaces
contents.reason: The selected surface example tests the orientable polygon attachment and fundamental class; adding the nonorientable genus family would duplicate the same matrix method without a downstream use.

contents.name: Example 2.38: An Acyclic Space
contents.reason: Its acyclic-but-noncontractible fundamental-group example is an application of a presentation complex rather than a needed step in the CW or cellular-homology construction.

contents.name: Example 2.39: the 3-torus
contents.reason: This separate multi-cell product calculation would duplicate the finite product-cell discussion without supporting a later claim in the pair.

contents.name: Example 2.40: Moore spaces
contents.reason: Realizing a prescribed cyclic homology group by an attaching degree is a useful construction, but it is neither a prerequisite nor one of the selected examples.

contents.name: Example 2.41: prescribed sequences of homology groups
contents.reason: The realization construction for arbitrary free chain complexes is a broader existence theorem than the selected computations and has no downstream dependency here.

contents.name: Example 2.42: real projective spaces
Example 2.43: lens spaces
Continuation of Example 2.43: infinite-dimensional lens spaces and their homology
contents.reason: The selected infinite calculation is for real projective space; the lens-space colimit variant would add another computation with no later use.

contents.name: Euler Characteristic
Theorem 2.44: the Euler-Poincare formula
Proposition 2.45: a finite-dimensional K(G,1) has torsionfree fundamental group
contents.reason: This is a group-theoretic obstruction obtained from the universal cover and lies beyond the pair's cellular-homology and finite-Euler scope.

Chapter 10, Section 1: Lemma that a pushout along a cellular map is a CW complex and its quotient complex is X/A

Chapter 10, Section 1: Lemma that products of CW complexes have product cells
Chapter 10, Section 1: Lemma that X times I is a CW complex relative to X times boundary I

Chapter 10, Section 3 "HELP and the Whitehead theorem": HELP and the two Whitehead theorems
contents.reason: HELP and Whitehead theorems depend on the higher-homotopy equivalence framework; cellular homology here uses only the cofibration and skeletal-homology consequences already proved directly.

contents.name: Chapter 10, Section 3: Theorem "Cellular approximation" and its corollary
contents.reason: Cellular approximation is a distinct homotopy-theoretic theorem whose proof needs the HELP connectivity setup; the live AT-12 page explicitly owns cellular approximation and its later Whitehead and Hurewicz uses.
